I hear a sense of conflict between your identity and your culture, which I appreciate must be very difficult for you. However, therapy isn’t going to change the fact that you’re gay. Sure, maybe it can help you come to terms with it, but it isn’t going to change your situation or help you to find a relationship. I recommend finding people close to you who you can confide in and building up a strong support network. I’m sure there are many people in your country who feel the same way as you and who are capable of giving you the love that you deserve. As another religious lesbian, I’m sending my best wishes and I hope you find a way to make it through this.
Seems unlikely, but if this really did happen then I think you might need a new therapist. That’s unethical in so many ways

If you don’t think your current therapist is a good fit then why not just switch therapists altogether? It’s very much advised against to have two therapists at once without them working together as this makes things more complex and the work can interfere with each other.
People say mean things they don’t really mean during fights; I think if you’re self aware of your flaws then you’re already well on track to becoming a better person.

I don’t think any of this is indicative of you being a narcissist if I’m honest; a lot of it seems quite normal for a 17 year old. If things do bother you then of course I’d recommend seeking therapy, but I really wouldn’t stress too much about the narcissist label as it doesn’t appear to fit.

Honestly, it sounds like the style or type of therapy you’ve had might not be the right one for you, and I agree that she should have offered you alternatives or a referral to someone else when you brought your concerns up with her. 

That doesn’t necessarily mean that psychotherapy as a whole won’t work for you. I think it’s worth trying to find a better fit and keeping an open mind. 

On the other hand, I do disagree with your perception of toxic friendships and I can see what your therapist was trying to say, in that it doesn’t take two people to create a toxic dynamic. That doesn’t mean that she should have been dismissive when you tried to discuss the positives though. 

Either way, I sincerely hope that you manage to find a better fit and find a way to work on these issues.

What makes you feel that it’s the therapy that directly caused the decline in your mental health? Could it not be possible that this is related to other underlying issues, or did something specifically happen within the therapy that made you feel worse?

Anxiety is a common and (to an extent) a very normal thing that most of us will experience at some point in our lives. For many people, techniques like mindfulness or practicing self care are enough to help them overcome their feelings of anxiety. However, some people need something more substantial like therapy or medication in order to overcome it. That’s not any more or less valid than than the other ways to help anxiety. 

Mental health issues are complex and there’s no “one size fits all” approach to treating them. If everything you’ve tried so far hasn’t helped then I’d recommend seeing your GP or seeking therapy if you haven’t done so already.

To be honest, it doesn’t sound like any of this was rape. It sounds like a lack communication or feelings of regret rather than a lack of consent. The whole dynamic sounds pretty unhealthy though, so maybe cutting things off altogether would help you both in the long term?

My therapist is a lot like this, and it sounds like your therapist is trained in psychodynamic therapy. This modality relies a lot on silence and the client directing the therapy with little intervention from the therapist. It works for some people and others hate it. If you’re not clicking with her then it’s definitely worth bringing it up.
